name: Creational Patterns
purpose: Object creation mechanisms that increase flexibility and reuse of existing code

patterns.name: Singleton
patterns.description:
Ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.
Prevents multiple instances of a class from being created, which is useful for managing shared resources.
Commonly used for database connections, logging, configuration management, and caching mechanisms.
Provides lazy initialization and thread-safe implementations for concurrent environments.
Should be used sparingly as it can make code harder to test and can hide dependencies.

patterns.name: Factory Method
patterns.description:
Provides an interface for creating objects without specifying their exact classes.
Allows subclasses to decide which class to instantiate, promoting loose coupling between creator and product.
Ideal for scenarios where you need to create objects based on runtime conditions or configuration.
Enables easy extension of the system with new product types without modifying existing code.
Commonly used in frameworks where framework classes need to create application-specific objects.

patterns.name: Abstract Factory
patterns.description:
Provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.
Groups related factory methods together to create objects that work together as a cohesive unit.
Useful when you need to ensure that created objects are compatible with each other.
Enables switching between entire families of products at runtime or configuration time.
Commonly used in UI frameworks, database drivers, and cross-platform development.

patterns.name: Builder
patterns.description:
Constructs complex objects step by step, allowing different representations using the same construction code.
Separates the construction of a complex object from its representation.
Enables building objects with many optional parameters in a readable and maintainable way.
Prevents telescoping constructor anti-pattern and provides fluent interface for object creation.
Ideal for creating objects with many configuration options, such as query builders or configuration objects.

patterns.name: Prototype
patterns.description:
Creates new objects by copying existing instances rather than creating new ones from scratch.
Allows adding and removing objects at runtime by cloning prototype instances.
Reduces the cost of creating objects, especially when object creation is expensive.
Enables dynamic configuration of objects by cloning and modifying prototype instances.
Commonly used when object creation is more expensive than copying, such as database queries or complex calculations.

patterns.name: Object Pool
patterns.description:
Maintains a pool of reusable objects to avoid expensive acquisition and release of resources.
Improves performance by reusing objects instead of creating and destroying them repeatedly.
Manages object lifecycle and ensures objects are properly initialized before reuse.
Useful for expensive-to-create objects like database connections, threads, or network connections.
Requires careful management to prevent resource leaks and ensure thread safety in concurrent environments.

name: Structural Patterns
purpose: Ways to compose objects and classes into larger structures while keeping them flexible and efficient

patterns.name: Adapter
patterns.description:
Allows incompatible interfaces to work together by wrapping an object with an adapter class.
Acts as a bridge between two incompatible interfaces, enabling them to collaborate.
Enables integration of third-party libraries or legacy code without modifying existing code.
Can be implemented as class adapter (using inheritance) or object adapter (using composition).
Commonly used when integrating new components into existing systems or working with external APIs.

patterns.name: Bridge
patterns.description:
Separates an object's abstraction from its implementation, allowing them to vary independently.
Prevents the exponential growth of classes when combining multiple dimensions of variation.
Enables runtime binding of implementations and promotes code organization through separation of concerns.
Useful when you need to avoid permanent binding between abstraction and implementation.
Commonly used in GUI frameworks, device drivers, and when supporting multiple platforms.

patterns.name: Composite
patterns.description:
Composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies.
Allows clients to treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.
Enables recursive composition and simplifies client code that works with complex tree structures.
Ideal for representing hierarchical structures like file systems, UI components, or organizational structures.
Provides a way to build complex objects from simpler ones while maintaining a consistent interface.

patterns.name: Decorator
patterns.description:
Attaches additional responsibilities to objects dynamically without altering their structure.
Provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.
Allows behavior to be added to individual objects without affecting other objects of the same class.
Enables composition of behaviors at runtime, providing more flexibility than static inheritance.
Commonly used for adding features like logging, caching, validation, or encryption to objects.

patterns.name: Facade
patterns.description:
Provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem, hiding its complexity.
Acts as a single entry point to a set of interfaces in a subsystem.
Reduces coupling between clients and subsystem components, making the system easier to use.
Does not prevent access to subsystem classes but provides a convenient higher-level interface.
Commonly used to simplify complex APIs, libraries, or frameworks for client applications.

patterns.name: Flyweight
patterns.description:
Minimizes memory usage by sharing intrinsic state among multiple objects.
Separates intrinsic (shared) state from extrinsic (context-specific) state.
Reduces memory footprint when dealing with large numbers of similar objects.
Useful when an application uses a large number of objects with shared characteristics.
Commonly used in text editors, game development, and applications with many similar objects.

patterns.name: Proxy
patterns.description:
Provides a placeholder or surrogate object that controls access to another object.
Acts as an intermediary between client and target object, adding an extra level of indirection.
Can provide lazy loading, access control, logging, or caching without changing the target object.
Enables adding cross-cutting concerns like security, performance, or monitoring transparently.
Commonly used for virtual proxies, protection proxies, remote proxies, and smart references.

name: Behavioral Patterns
purpose: Communication patterns between objects and assignment of responsibilities

patterns.name: Chain of Responsibility
patterns.description:
Passes requests along a chain of handlers until one handles the request.
Decouples the sender of a request from its receiver by giving multiple objects a chance to handle it.
Allows you to add or remove handlers dynamically without modifying the client code.
Useful for processing requests that can be handled by multiple objects in a specific order.
Commonly used in event handling systems, middleware, and validation pipelines.

patterns.name: Command
patterns.description:
Encapsulates a request as an object, allowing parameterization and queuing of requests.
Turns requests into objects, enabling undo/redo functionality and request queuing.
Decouples the object that invokes the operation from the object that performs it.
Enables logging, queuing, and scheduling of operations, as well as supporting transactions.
Commonly used in GUI applications, macro recording, and implementing undo/redo functionality.

patterns.name: Iterator
patterns.description:
Provides a way to access elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.
Encapsulates the traversal logic and provides a uniform interface for iterating over different collections.
Enables multiple traversals of the same collection simultaneously and supports different iteration algorithms.
Simplifies collection interfaces by removing traversal methods from collection classes.
Commonly used in collection frameworks, database result sets, and tree traversal algorithms.

patterns.name: Mediator
patterns.description:
Defines an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, promoting loose coupling.
Centralizes complex communications and control logic between objects.
Reduces dependencies between communicating objects, making the system easier to understand and maintain.
Prevents objects from referring to each other explicitly, reducing coupling.
Commonly used in GUI frameworks, chat applications, and systems with many interacting components.

patterns.name: Memento
patterns.description:
Captures and externalizes an object's internal state so it can be restored later.
Enables saving and restoring object state without violating encapsulation.
Allows objects to return to previous states without exposing implementation details.
Useful for implementing undo/redo functionality, checkpoints, and state snapshots.
Commonly used in text editors, games, and applications requiring state management.

patterns.name: Observer
patterns.description:
Defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all dependents are notified.
Enables loose coupling between subject and observers, allowing dynamic subscription and unsubscription.
Supports broadcast communication and enables objects to be notified of changes without tight coupling.
Ideal for implementing event-driven architectures and model-view separation.
Commonly used in MVC architectures, event handling systems, and publish-subscribe mechanisms.

patterns.name: State
patterns.description:
Allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes, appearing to change its class.
Encapsulates state-specific behavior and transitions between states in separate classes.
Eliminates large conditional statements and makes state transitions explicit and manageable.
Enables adding new states and transitions without modifying existing code.
Commonly used in state machines, workflow engines, and objects with complex state-dependent behavior.

patterns.name: Strategy
patterns.description:
Defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable.
Enables selecting algorithms at runtime and makes algorithms independent of the clients that use them.
Allows algorithms to vary independently from clients that use them, promoting the Open/Closed Principle.
Eliminates conditional statements for algorithm selection and enables easy extension with new algorithms.
Commonly used for sorting algorithms, compression algorithms, and payment processing systems.

patterns.name: Template Method
patterns.description:
Defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, letting subclasses override specific steps.
Enables code reuse by defining invariant parts of an algorithm once in a base class.
Allows subclasses to customize specific steps while maintaining the overall algorithm structure.
Promotes the Hollywood Principle: 'Don't call us, we'll call you'.
Commonly used in frameworks, where framework classes define the algorithm structure and application classes provide specific implementations.

patterns.name: Visitor
patterns.description:
Separates algorithms from the objects on which they operate.
Allows adding new operations to object structures without modifying the classes of the objects.
Enables operations to be defined externally and applied to different object types.
Useful when you have many unrelated operations to perform on object structures.
Commonly used in compiler design, abstract syntax trees, and when operations need to be added to stable class hierarchies.

name: Concurrency Patterns
purpose: Patterns for managing concurrent execution and thread safety

patterns.name: Active Object
patterns.description:
Decouples method execution from method invocation for objects that each reside in their own thread of control.
Encapsulates requests as objects and executes them asynchronously in a separate thread.
Enables method calls to return immediately while operations execute in the background.
Provides thread-safe access to objects and prevents blocking of calling threads.
Commonly used in GUI applications, network servers, and systems requiring responsive user interfaces.

patterns.name: Balking
patterns.description:
Prevents an object from executing an action if it is in an inappropriate state.
Allows an object to refuse to execute an operation if certain conditions are not met.
Prevents unnecessary work and potential errors by checking preconditions before execution.
Useful for operations that should only execute under specific conditions.
Commonly used in initialization patterns, resource management, and state-dependent operations.

patterns.name: Barrier
patterns.description:
Synchronizes a group of threads, forcing them to wait until all threads reach a certain point.
Ensures that all participating threads have completed a phase before proceeding to the next phase.
Useful for parallel algorithms that require synchronization at specific points.
Enables coordination of multiple threads working on different parts of a problem.
Commonly used in parallel processing, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and multi-phase computations.

patterns.name: Double-Checked Locking
patterns.description:
Reduces the overhead of acquiring a lock by first testing the locking criterion without actually acquiring the lock.
Optimizes performance by avoiding synchronization when it's not needed.
Requires careful implementation to ensure thread safety and prevent race conditions.
Useful for lazy initialization in multi-threaded environments where initialization is expensive.
Must be implemented correctly to avoid subtle bugs related to memory visibility and instruction reordering.

patterns.name: Guarded Suspension
patterns.description:
Manages operations that require both a lock to be acquired and a precondition to be satisfied.
Suspends thread execution until the precondition becomes true, then proceeds with the operation.
Prevents busy waiting and ensures threads only proceed when conditions are met.
Useful for producer-consumer scenarios and operations that depend on resource availability.
Commonly used in bounded buffers, thread pools, and resource management systems.

patterns.name: Lock
patterns.description:
Synchronizes access to shared resources by acquiring and releasing locks.
Prevents multiple threads from accessing critical sections simultaneously.
Ensures mutual exclusion and prevents race conditions in concurrent programs.
Can be implemented as mutexes, read-write locks, or semaphores depending on requirements.
Essential for thread-safe programming but requires careful use to avoid deadlocks and performance issues.

patterns.name: Monitor Object
patterns.description:
Synchronizes concurrent method execution to ensure only one method runs within an object at a time.
Encapsulates synchronization logic within the object itself.
Provides a structured approach to thread-safe object design.
Enables safe concurrent access to object state through synchronized methods.
Commonly used in concurrent data structures and thread-safe collections.

patterns.name: Producer-Consumer
patterns.description:
Separates the identification of work to be done from the execution of that work.
Uses a shared buffer or queue to decouple producers and consumers.
Enables asynchronous processing and load balancing between producers and consumers.
Allows producers and consumers to operate at different rates without blocking each other.
Commonly used in message queues, event-driven systems, and parallel processing pipelines.

patterns.name: Read-Write Lock
patterns.description:
Allows multiple readers or a single writer to access a shared resource.
Optimizes performance for read-heavy workloads by allowing concurrent reads.
Ensures exclusive access for write operations while enabling concurrent read operations.
Improves throughput in scenarios where reads are more frequent than writes.
Commonly used in database systems, caching mechanisms, and shared data structures.

patterns.name: Thread Pool
patterns.description:
Maintains a group of worker threads that execute tasks from a queue.
Reuses threads to avoid the overhead of thread creation and destruction.
Limits the number of concurrent threads and manages resource consumption.
Enables efficient task execution and provides better control over system resources.
Commonly used in web servers, application servers, and systems requiring efficient task processing.

name: Architectural Patterns
purpose: High-level patterns for structuring applications and systems

patterns.name: Model-View-Controller (MVC)
patterns.description:
Separates application logic into three interconnected components: Model, View, and Controller.
Model manages data and business logic, View handles presentation, and Controller processes user input.
Promotes separation of concerns and enables independent development and testing of components.
Allows multiple views of the same data and supports change propagation through the Observer pattern.
Commonly used in web frameworks, desktop applications, and mobile app development.

patterns.name: Model-View-Presenter (MVP)
patterns.description:
Variation of MVC where the Presenter handles all user input and updates the View.
View is passive and delegates all user interactions to the Presenter.
Improves testability by making the View easily mockable and moving logic to the Presenter.
Enables better separation between presentation logic and view implementation.
Commonly used in desktop applications, Android development, and when testability is a priority.

patterns.name: Model-View-ViewModel (MVVM)
patterns.description:
Separates the development of graphical user interface from business logic through data binding.
ViewModel exposes data and commands that the View can bind to, enabling two-way data binding.
Reduces code-behind in views and promotes testable, maintainable code.
Enables declarative UI development and automatic synchronization between View and ViewModel.
Commonly used in WPF, Angular, Vue.js, and modern frontend frameworks.

patterns.name: Layered Architecture
patterns.description:
Organizes application into horizontal layers, each with a specific responsibility.
Typically includes presentation, business logic, data access, and database layers.
Enables separation of concerns and provides clear boundaries between different aspects of the application.
Allows layers to be developed, tested, and maintained independently.
Commonly used in enterprise applications, web applications, and systems requiring clear separation of concerns.

patterns.name: Microservices
patterns.description:
Structures an application as a collection of loosely coupled, independently deployable services.
Each service is responsible for a specific business capability and communicates via well-defined APIs.
Enables independent scaling, deployment, and technology choices for each service.
Improves fault isolation and allows teams to work independently on different services.
Commonly used in cloud-native applications, large-scale systems, and when services need independent evolution.

patterns.name: Event-Driven Architecture
patterns.description:
Uses events to trigger and communicate between decoupled services.
Services produce and consume events asynchronously, enabling loose coupling.
Allows services to react to events without direct dependencies on event producers.
Enables scalable, responsive systems and supports real-time processing.
Commonly used in distributed systems, IoT applications, and systems requiring high responsiveness.

patterns.name: Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)
patterns.description:
Structures applications as a collection of services that communicate over a network.
Services are self-contained, reusable, and expose well-defined interfaces.
Enables integration of disparate systems and promotes service reuse across applications.
Supports loose coupling and enables services to be developed and deployed independently.
Commonly used in enterprise integration, legacy system modernization, and distributed systems.

patterns.name: Repository
patterns.description:
Mediates between the domain and data mapping layers, acting like an in-memory domain object collection.
Encapsulates the logic needed to access data sources and provides a more object-oriented view.
Enables separation of business logic from data access logic and improves testability.
Allows switching between different data sources without changing business logic.
Commonly used in domain-driven design, data access layers, and when abstracting persistence mechanisms.

patterns.name: Unit of Work
patterns.description:
Maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates writing out changes.
Tracks changes to objects and ensures consistency when committing transactions.
Prevents duplicate updates and manages the lifecycle of objects within a transaction.
Enables atomic operations and provides a clean way to manage database transactions.
Commonly used with the Repository pattern in data access layers and ORM frameworks.

patterns.name: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
patterns.description:
Separates read and write operations into different models and potentially different data stores.
Commands modify state while queries return data, enabling independent optimization.
Allows scaling read and write operations independently and using different technologies.
Enables event sourcing and provides better performance for read-heavy or write-heavy workloads.
Commonly used in complex domain models, high-performance systems, and when read and write patterns differ significantly.

name: Design Principles
purpose: Fundamental principles that guide good software design

patterns.name: SOLID Principles
patterns.description:
Five object-oriented design principles that make software designs more understandable, flexible, and maintainable.
Single Responsibility: A class should have only one reason to change.
Open/Closed: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.
Liskov Substitution: Objects should be replaceable with instances of their subtypes.
Interface Segregation: Clients should not depend on interfaces they don't use.
Dependency Inversion: Depend on abstractions, not concretions.

patterns.name: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)
patterns.description:
Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous representation within a system.
Eliminates code duplication and reduces maintenance burden.
Promotes code reuse and ensures consistency across the codebase.
When information needs to change, it only needs to be updated in one place.
Applied at multiple levels: functions, classes, modules, and even documentation.

patterns.name: KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid)
patterns.description:
Simplicity should be a key goal in design, and unnecessary complexity should be avoided.
Encourages straightforward solutions over complex ones when both achieve the same goal.
Reduces the likelihood of bugs and makes code easier to understand and maintain.
Promotes clarity and readability, which are essential for long-term project success.
Reminds developers that the simplest solution that works is often the best solution.

patterns.name: YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)
patterns.description:
Don't add functionality until it is actually necessary.
Prevents over-engineering and unnecessary complexity.
Focuses development effort on current requirements rather than speculative features.
Reduces code bloat and maintenance burden by avoiding premature optimization.
Encourages iterative development and adding features only when they provide immediate value.

patterns.name: Separation of Concerns
patterns.description:
Divides a computer program into distinct sections that address separate concerns.
Each section addresses a separate aspect of the program's functionality.
Enables independent development, testing, and maintenance of different parts.
Reduces coupling between components and improves code organization.
Applied at multiple levels: functions, classes, modules, layers, and architectural boundaries.

patterns.name: Composition Over Inheritance
patterns.description:
Favors object composition over class inheritance for code reuse.
Composition provides more flexibility and avoids the limitations of inheritance hierarchies.
Enables runtime behavior modification and avoids the fragile base class problem.
Promotes loose coupling and follows the 'has-a' relationship instead of 'is-a'.
Commonly used to achieve polymorphism and code reuse without inheritance constraints.

patterns.name: Program to Interfaces, Not Implementations
patterns.description:
Depend on abstractions rather than concrete implementations.
Enables flexibility and makes code easier to modify and extend.
Allows swapping implementations without changing dependent code.
Promotes loose coupling and supports the Dependency Inversion Principle.
Essential for creating testable, maintainable, and extensible software systems.

patterns.name: Favor Immutability
patterns.description:
Prefer immutable objects that cannot be modified after creation.
Eliminates many concurrency issues by preventing state changes.
Makes code easier to reason about and reduces bugs related to state mutation.
Enables safe sharing of objects and simplifies parallel programming.
Commonly used in functional programming and when thread safety is important.

patterns.name: Fail Fast
patterns.description:
Detect and report errors as early as possible, preferably at compile time.
Prevents errors from propagating through the system and becoming harder to diagnose.
Enables immediate feedback and makes debugging easier.
Encourages strong typing, validation, and explicit error handling.
Improves system reliability by catching problems before they cause larger issues.

patterns.name: Principle of Least Surprise
patterns.description:
Design systems to behave in ways that users expect, based on their prior experience.
Makes software more intuitive and easier to learn.
Reduces cognitive load and improves user experience.
Applies to API design, user interfaces, and system behavior.
Encourages consistency and following established conventions and patterns.

name: Anti-Patterns
purpose: Common solutions that are counterproductive and should be avoided

patterns.name: God Object
patterns.description:
An object that knows too much or does too much, violating the Single Responsibility Principle.
Centralizes too much functionality in a single class, making it difficult to understand and maintain.
Creates tight coupling and makes the system brittle to changes.
Makes testing difficult and reduces code reusability.
Solution: Break down into smaller, focused classes with single responsibilities.

patterns.name: Spaghetti Code
patterns.description:
Code with a complex and tangled control structure, making it difficult to follow the program flow.
Lacks clear structure and organization, making maintenance extremely difficult.
Often results from quick fixes and lack of refactoring over time.
Makes debugging challenging and increases the likelihood of introducing bugs.
Solution: Refactor into well-structured code with clear separation of concerns.

patterns.name: Copy-Paste Programming
patterns.description:
Copying existing code and modifying it instead of creating reusable components.
Violates the DRY principle and leads to code duplication.
Increases maintenance burden as bugs must be fixed in multiple places.
Makes it difficult to ensure consistency across duplicated code.
Solution: Extract common functionality into reusable functions, classes, or modules.

patterns.name: Golden Hammer
patterns.description:
Over-reliance on a familiar tool or technology, applying it to every problem.
Forces solutions into patterns that may not be appropriate for the problem.
Prevents exploring better alternatives and can lead to over-engineering.
Limits the developer's ability to choose the right tool for each situation.
Solution: Evaluate each problem independently and choose appropriate tools and patterns.

patterns.name: Premature Optimization
patterns.description:
Optimizing code before identifying actual performance bottlenecks.
Wastes development time on optimizations that may not be needed.
Often makes code more complex and harder to maintain without significant benefit.
Can introduce bugs and make the codebase more difficult to understand.
Solution: Measure first, optimize only when necessary, and focus on clear, maintainable code.

patterns.name: Cargo Cult Programming
patterns.description:
Using patterns and practices without understanding why they are used.
Applies solutions blindly without considering if they fit the problem.
Leads to unnecessary complexity and can introduce problems rather than solve them.
Prevents learning and understanding of underlying principles.
Solution: Understand the reasoning behind patterns and practices before applying them.

patterns.name: Magic Numbers
patterns.description:
Using unexplained numeric or string literals directly in code.
Makes code difficult to understand and maintain.
Hides the meaning and purpose of values, making debugging harder.
Makes it difficult to change values consistently across the codebase.
Solution: Use named constants or configuration values with clear, descriptive names.

patterns.name: Hard Coding
patterns.description:
Embedding configuration data or business logic directly in source code.
Makes it difficult to change behavior without modifying and recompiling code.
Reduces flexibility and makes the system less adaptable to different environments.
Violates separation of concerns by mixing configuration with implementation.
Solution: Externalize configuration to files, environment variables, or configuration systems.

patterns.name: Feature Envy
patterns.description:
A method that is more interested in another class's data than its own.
Indicates that the method might belong in the other class.
Creates unnecessary coupling and violates encapsulation.
Makes code organization unclear and can lead to maintenance issues.
Solution: Move the method to the class whose data it primarily uses, or refactor to reduce coupling.

patterns.name: Lava Flow
patterns.description:
Dead code and forgotten design decisions that remain in the codebase.
Accumulates over time as features are added and removed without cleanup.
Makes the codebase larger and more confusing than necessary.
Hides important code and makes maintenance more difficult.
Solution: Regularly refactor and remove unused code, keeping the codebase clean and maintainable.
